prompt.context: Your client is a large pharmaceutical company based in Ibiza looking to develop a marketing plan for its new prescription dietary drug (Product X). It is set to launch within the next few months. Weight loss is a new space for your client, and they are relying on you to help them construct a plan.
prompt.question: What types of things would you first consider as you begin to develop your marketing plan?

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's primary goal?
clarifying_info.a: To increase total prescriptions written for Product X.

clarifying_info.q: Is there competition in this space?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, there is one other well-known competitor with considerable market share.

clarifying_info.q: How does the client's product compare to the competitor?
clarifying_info.a: Product X has been shown to be more efficacious and has a better dosing schedule than the competitor's drug.

clarifying_info.q: Where is the product being marketed?
clarifying_info.a: The client is based in Ibiza but is marketing this product within the US.

clarifying_info.q: Is cost a constraint for the marketing effort?
clarifying_info.a: No. Cost is not a primary consideration; the client has set aside a large investment and expects significant costs, with the hope that the product can offset them.

exhibits.title: Number of Doctors within Each Quartile
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the number of Specialists and PCPs within each of the four quartiles (Q1 through Q4).
exhibits.data: Bar chart with two series (Specialists and PCPs) across quartiles 1-4; y-axis from 0 to 450; footnote: Q1 is the highest projected prescribers, Q4 the lowest.

exhibits.title: Patient and Prescription Data by Quartile
exhibits.shows: Two tables (one for Specialists, one for PCPs) showing, for each quartile: number of total patients per doctor, percent of patients eligible for Product X, and percent of eligible patients likely to be prescribed Product X by the doctor.

framework: Customers: How to segment the customer pool (prescribers vs. end consumers), and within prescribers how to prioritize by specialty, geography, prescribing behavior, patient population, or existing relationships
Channel: Which channels to use to reach customers (TV, online/digital, print, email, in-office sales reps, medical journals, conferences, etc.)
Content/Messaging: What messages to carry — highlight Product X's efficacy and dosing advantages over the competitor
Competition: Who the competitor is, how they are marketing, and where gaps or differentiation opportunities exist
Cadence: How frequently to reach out and whether to sequence channels in a particular order
Other considerations: Government regulations on pharmaceutical advertising, internal coordination across teams, pricing/cost/revenue model, the broader healthcare ecosystem

questions.prompt: What are some ways you could segment potential customers (doctors) for Product X?
questions.guidance: Candidate should produce at least four segmentation dimensions in a structured manner. Strong answers include: geography (region, urban vs. rural); specialty (dieticians, PCPs, other specialists); prescribing behavior (high vs. low prescribers); marketing engagement/channel receptivity (digital vs. print); patient population size (high vs. low number of eligible patients); previous relationships (existing vs. new clients).

questions.prompt: Given Exhibit 1, which quartile of doctors would you target and why? (Note: you must choose one quartile and target both Specialists and PCPs within it.)
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate total expected prescriptions for Specialists and PCPs in each quartile, then sum them to identify the quartile with the highest combined total. Q1 produces the highest total prescriptions and should be selected. Candidate should walk through the multiplication clearly and round numbers where helpful.

math.setup: For each quartile and doctor type: Total Rx = (patients per doctor) x (% eligible) x (% prescribed) x (number of doctors). Sum Specialist Rx + PCP Rx per quartile.
steps: Specialists Q1: 360 x 60% = 216 eligible; 216 x 75% = 162 prescribed per doctor; 162 x 150 doctors = 24,300 Rx
math.answer: Q1 yields the highest total prescriptions (41,740) and should be the target quartile.

questions.prompt: What types of marketing channels and tactics would you use to reach the Q1 target physicians? Would you deploy any channels first or in a particular sequence?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm channels relevant to pharmaceutical marketing to physicians. Strong answers reference channels mentioned in the framework. There is no single right answer on sequencing, but the candidate should justify their prioritization logic (e.g., start with sales rep visits for high-touch relationship-building, then layer in digital for scale).

brainstorming.prompt: What are some ways you could segment potential customers (doctors) for Product X?

categories.name: Geography
ideas: State-level regulatory or prescribing environment differences

categories.name: Prescribing Behavior
ideas: High prescribers vs. low prescribers of comparable drugs
Quartile segmentation based on projected likelihood to prescribe Product X

categories.name: Marketing Engagement / Channel Receptivity
ideas: Receptive to digital/online outreach vs. print and in-office materials

categories.name: Patient Population
ideas: Doctors with a high volume of eligible patients
Doctors serving populations with high obesity/weight-loss need

categories.name: Existing Relationships
ideas: Doctors client already has a relationship with (lower acquisition cost)
New-to-client doctors (higher potential upside but higher cost to reach)

recommendation: Target Q1 Specialists and PCPs because this quartile offers the greatest total prescription potential (41,740 Rx), exceeding Q2 (39,600), Q3 (35,262), and Q4 (32,718).

To reach Q1 targets, deploy a focused multi-channel approach: prioritize in-office sales representative visits for high-touch engagement, supplement with targeted digital tactics (search display, MD-specific website banners, Product X brand website), and use journal article ads and medical conferences to build credibility.

Excellent candidates note spillover effects: marketing efforts aimed at Q1 will incidentally reach Q2-Q4 physicians through the same channels, generating incremental prescriptions beyond the primary target.
risks: Projections underlying the quartile model should be validated with additional market research before committing the full budget.
Need to confirm that the selected channels can actually reach Q1 physicians at the anticipated scale.
Competitor response: the incumbent with considerable market share may intensify marketing in response to Product X's launch.
Regulatory risks around pharmaceutical advertising (FDA guidelines on prescription drug promotion) must be assessed.
Client lacks experience in weight loss — internal capability and knowledge gaps need to be addressed.
next_steps: Validate prescription projection assumptions through additional market research.
Identify and finalize key messages that communicate Product X's efficacy and dosing advantages to Q1 targets.
Map which specific channels Q1 Specialists and PCPs are most receptive to and build an engagement calendar.
Analyze competitor marketing tactics to identify differentiation opportunities.
Assess regulatory requirements for all planned promotional materials and channels.
Determine revenue/cost model to confirm the marketing investment is on track to be offset by projected prescription volume.
